# What is newly arrived in the OpenAI “family” relevant to AI Agents / MCP

Below is the practical update view — only things that matter for your exploration.

## 1. Responses API became the main base layer for agent-like apps

OpenAI positions the **Responses API** as the unified interface for building agent-like applications, with built-in tools, multi-turn continuity, multimodal support, and remote MCP support. That means, in practical terms, a lot of the “agent stack” now centers around Responses rather than older fragmented patterns. citeturn502622search14turn502622search2

### Why this matters
Earlier, people used separate patterns for plain chat, tools, orchestration, and custom wrappers.  
Now the direction is more like:

```text
Model
+ Tools
+ Memory / state
+ MCP
+ Orchestration
= agent system
```

This is one of the biggest practical shifts. citeturn502622search7turn502622search14

---

## 2. Built-in tools became first-class

OpenAI’s agent/tool stack now treats tools like:

- web search
- file search
- computer use
- code interpreter
- remote MCP servers

as standard extensions to model capability, instead of one-off hacks. The tools guide and Responses guide both show this clearly. citeturn502622search17turn502622search14

### Why this matters
This is the real difference between:

- **LLM answering**
- **agent doing work**

Because the model is no longer limited to text-only reasoning; it can work through tools in a structured way. citeturn502622search15turn502622search17

---

## 3. MCP is now treated as a serious bridge, not just a side concept

OpenAI now has explicit docs for:

- **building remote MCP servers**
- **using MCP and connectors**
- **using MCP in Realtime sessions**
- **using MCP with ChatGPT apps and API integrations** citeturn502622search1turn502622search5turn502622search9

### Practical meaning
MCP is becoming the standard way to give models structured access to:

- company data
- external systems
- tools
- business actions

without stuffing everything into prompts. citeturn502622search1turn502622search5

So MCP is no longer “just an idea.”  
It is now part of the actual product direction.

---

## 4. Agent Builder is a major practical addition

OpenAI’s **Agent Builder** is now the visual workflow layer for building agents. The docs describe workflows as combinations of agents, tools, and control-flow logic, with design, preview, publish, and deployment flow. citeturn502622search3

### Why this matters
This is important for people like you because it moves the stack from:

> “code everything from scratch”

to

> “design the workflow clearly first”

That means agent building is becoming more like **system design** and less like prompt-only experimentation. citeturn502622search3turn502622search11

---

## 5. ChatKit is part of the embedded-agent story

OpenAI’s current stack includes **ChatKit** as the UI layer for embedding an agent experience into a product, and the public showcase shows it being used with the Agents SDK for app-like experiences. citeturn502622search4

### Why this matters
This means the stack is now clearly split into layers:

| Layer | OpenAI piece |
|---|---|
| Build workflow | Agent Builder |
| Run orchestration | Responses API / Agents SDK |
| Connect systems | MCP / connectors |
| Put in product UI | ChatKit |

That layering is much clearer now than before. citeturn502622search3turn502622search5turn502622search4

---

## 6. Apps SDK keeps expanding around ChatGPT-native apps

The **Apps SDK** continues to change actively, and its March 2026 changelog shows ongoing additions such as file-library helpers and plugin distribution guidance. That tells you the “build apps for ChatGPT” side is still moving and being actively shaped. citeturn502622search16

### Practical meaning
There are really two broad roads now:

1. **Build your own product with OpenAI agent stack**
2. **Build something that plugs into ChatGPT**

Both are alive, but they are not the same thing. citeturn502622search16turn502622search1

---

## 7. Realtime + MCP is now a direct pattern

OpenAI also documents **Realtime API with MCP**, where MCP tools can be attached directly to a live conversation session. citeturn502622search9

### Why this matters
This opens a practical future pattern like:

```text
Voice conversation
→ model reasons live
→ MCP tool gets called
→ system returns result
→ model continues speaking
```

So the agent world is no longer only text-chat-based. citeturn502622search9

---

## 8. Newer model releases also matter for agents

As of March 2026, OpenAI’s changelog shows newer model releases including **GPT-5.4**, **GPT-5.4 pro**, **GPT-5.4 mini**, and **GPT-5.4 nano** across Responses and/or Chat Completions, with positioning from frontier/pro work down to smaller high-volume usage. citeturn502622search0

### Why this matters
In agent systems, model choice increasingly becomes:

- heavy reasoning model for hard tasks
- lighter cheaper model for repeated operational steps

That is useful for real systems, because not every task should use the most expensive brain. citeturn502622search0turn502622search7

---

# So what changed in simple words?

## Earlier
- chatbot
- prompt engineering
- manual integrations
- lots of glue code

## Now
- workflow design
- tool-using agents
- MCP / connectors
- embedded product UI
- tracing / evals / orchestration

OpenAI’s current “building agents” material makes that direction very explicit. citeturn502622search7turn502622search11

Page: 00000-03-AIAgent-vs-Scheduler  

---

# 1. Core Difference (one-line clarity)

> **Scheduler = “When to run”**  
> **AI Agent = “What to do + how to decide”**

---

# 2. Simple Analogy (real-world)

| Concept | Real World |
|--------|-----------|
| Scheduler | Alarm clock ⏰ |
| AI Agent | Assistant 👤 |

- Alarm rings at 6 AM → fixed  
- Assistant decides:
  - wake you  
  - reschedule if tired  
  - cancel if holiday  

---

# 3. Technical Difference

## Scheduler

### What it does:
- Runs **predefined task**
- At **fixed time / trigger**

### Example:
```text
Every day 13:30 → send market report
```

👉 No thinking  
👉 No decision  
👉 Just execution

---

## AI Agent

### What it does:
- Understands input
- Decides action
- Can adapt

### Example:
```text
Read message →
Is it task? →
If yes → create task →
If urgent → notify →
If unclear → ask question
```

👉 Has logic + reasoning  
👉 Can change behaviour  

---

# 4. Side-by-side Comparison

| Aspect | Scheduler | AI Agent |
|-------|----------|----------|
| Intelligence | None | Yes |
| Flexibility | Fixed | Dynamic |
| Input handling | None / simple trigger | Complex (text, voice) |
| Decision making | ❌ | ✅ |
| Error handling | Fails silently | Can adapt / ask |
| Use case | Repeating jobs | Real-world workflows |

---

# 5. In YOUR System (WE MD context)

## Scheduler Example

- Daily 9 PM:
  - Send reminder: “Update expenses”

👉 Same message every day  
👉 No context awareness  

---

## AI Agent Example

- Reads:
  > “Money given to Valli attan”

Agent:

1. Detects → financial event  
2. Checks → was approval done?  
3. If no → flags issue  
4. Logs entry  
5. Notifies you  

👉 This is **governance + intelligence**

---

# 6. Where people get confused

Many tools say:

> “AI automation”

But actually they are:

❌ Scheduler + template  
✅ Not real AI Agent  

---

# 7. Best Practice (important for you)

## Do NOT replace scheduler

Instead:

### Use both together

``` id="k9v7sz"
Scheduler → triggers
AI Agent → decides + acts
MCP → controls rules
```

---

### Example (your future system)

- **Scheduler**
  → 13:30 daily trigger  

- **AI Agent**
  → Collect data  
  → Validate  
  → Generate report  

- **MCP**
  → Ensure:
    - correct format  
    - approval  
    - trace stored  

---

# 8. Advantages vs Risks

## Scheduler

### ✅
- Reliable
- Predictable
- Simple

### ❌
- Dumb
- Cannot adapt
- No understanding

---

## AI Agent

### ✅
- Smart
- Context-aware
- Reduces your thinking load

### ❌
- Can make mistakes
- Needs control (very important for finance/trust)
- Requires MCP layer

---

# 9. Final Insight (this matters)

> Scheduler is **time-based automation**  
> AI Agent is **decision-based automation**

---

## Your System Evolution

You are moving from:

> Manual → Scheduler → AI Agent → MCP-controlled system

---

If you want next clarity:

👉 **“Show real example: Scheduler + AI Agent + MCP working together in WE MD”**

That will make this 100% concrete for your use case.

# WE MD mapped to the exact OpenAI stack

I’ll map this in a **practical rollout**, not a fancy architecture dream.

## The OpenAI stack pieces we are using

| Stack piece | What it does in your WE MD system |
|---|---|
| **Agent Builder** | Design and test the workflow visually |
| **ChatKit** | Give WE MD a usable chat interface inside your own app/site |
| **Responses API / Agents SDK** | Run the real backend orchestration and tool-calling |
| **MCP server / connectors** | Connect the agent to Sheets, approvals, documents, finance logs, task systems |
| **Tracing / evals** | Review what the agent did and improve reliability |
| **Approval-gated tools** | Prevent dangerous automatic actions |

OpenAI’s current docs position Agent Builder as the workflow design canvas, ChatKit as the embedded chat experience, Agents SDK as the orchestration layer, and MCP/connectors as the way to give the model access to external capabilities. They also emphasize traces, evals, and careful MCP tool use for safety. citeturn956612search0turn956612search1turn956612search2turn956612search3turn956612search11

---

# First: what WE MD actually needs

Based on your own stated WE MD needs, the operational core is:

- communication intake
- task tracking
- financial flow visibility
- approvals
- accountability

That means your first system should **not** be a general-purpose agent. It should be a **controlled operations agent** that turns messy communication into structured records, then helps humans review and act. This is exactly the kind of tool-using, workflow-based pattern OpenAI’s agent stack is built for. citeturn956612search3turn956612search6turn956612search17

---

# Phase 1 — Capture and structure work

## Goal of Phase 1

Turn informal WE MD communication into **clean operational records**.

This phase is about **intake**, not automation-heavy execution.

## What users do in Phase 1

Subha Sister / WE MD staff type or paste things like:

- “Need to follow up with donor”
- “Account opening still pending”
- “Money given for X purpose”
- “Call this person tomorrow”
- “This approval is waiting”

## What the system does

The agent reads the message and converts it into structured output such as:

- category
- task / non-task
- priority
- owner
- due date if mentioned
- approval needed or not
- finance-related or not
- source message reference

This is a very natural fit for an agent workflow designed in **Agent Builder** and later run through the **Responses API / Agents SDK**, because OpenAI’s stack is built around workflows, typed inputs/outputs, tool use, and traces. citeturn956612search0turn956612search2turn956612search6

## Practical OpenAI components in Phase 1

### 1) Agent Builder
Use Agent Builder first to define the intake workflow visually.

Example node flow:

```text
Incoming message
→ classify message
→ extract fields
→ decide if task / finance / approval / note
→ prepare structured record
→ send to storage tool
```

Agent Builder is explicitly documented as a visual canvas for composing workflows with nodes and connections, previewing them, and publishing versions. citeturn956612search0turn956612search20

### 2) Responses API or Agents SDK
Once the workflow is stable, run it from your own backend using the Responses API or Agents SDK.

This is the right move because OpenAI positions the Responses API for new agent-like applications and the Agents SDK for orchestration, handoffs, streaming, and full traces. citeturn956612search2turn956612search4turn956612search9

### 3) MCP server
Expose your first WE MD tools through an MCP server.

For Phase 1, the MCP tools should be **read-light and write-safe**, such as:

- `create_task_record`
- `append_activity_log`
- `save_finance_note`
- `save_approval_request`
- `fetch_today_pending_items`

OpenAI’s MCP/connectors docs describe remote MCP servers as the structured way to give the model access to external tools and services, and OpenAI’s Apps/MCP docs emphasize clear tool definitions. citeturn956612search3turn956612search7turn956612search16turn956612search23

## WE MD systems to connect in Phase 1

Keep it minimal:

| System | Why it exists in Phase 1 |
|---|---|
| **Google Sheet / Excel-like backend** | Simple structured storage |
| **Document repository** | Store notes, proofs, message references |
| **Activity log** | Keep audit trail |
| **Basic task list** | Show pending items |

## What not to do in Phase 1

Do **not** allow the agent to:

- transfer money
- approve disbursements
- send final official messages automatically
- modify financial records without review

OpenAI’s safety guidance specifically calls out risks around agent workflows and MCP tool calling, so this phase should stay conservative. citeturn956612search11turn956612search3

## Outcome of Phase 1

At the end of Phase 1, WE MD gets:

- one structured intake path
- one task register
- one finance-note register
- one approval-request register
- one activity timeline

This is the first real shift from **memory-based operations** to **system-based operations**.

---

# Phase 2 — Add review, approvals, and guided action

## Goal of Phase 2

Move from “capture the work” to “manage the work.”

Now the system should help WE MD **review**, **triage**, and **route** operational items.

## What users do in Phase 2

Instead of only pasting messages, users now also ask:

- “What is pending today?”
- “Which finance items need approval?”
- “Show all blocked tasks”
- “Which donor follow-ups are overdue?”
- “What happened this week?”

## What the system does

The agent can now:

- retrieve structured records
- group them by category/status
- identify overdue items
- surface approval queues
- prepare summaries for you and for Subha Sister
- draft messages or reminders for human review

This is where **ChatKit** becomes useful, because OpenAI documents it as the embedded chat layer for using an agent workflow in your own product. It is a good fit when staff need a practical interface instead of developer-facing tools. citeturn956612search1turn956612search5

## Practical OpenAI components in Phase 2

### 1) ChatKit frontend
Use ChatKit as the WE MD operations interface.

Why this matters in your case:

- Subha Sister should not need to understand API concepts
- staff can ask plain-language questions
- the UI can later add buttons, widgets, or actions

OpenAI’s ChatKit docs describe embedding chat workflows in your frontend, and the actions/widgets docs show how interactions can trigger backend work beyond just a typed message. citeturn956612search1turn956612search8turn956612search15

### 2) Agents SDK on backend
Now use the Agents SDK more actively for orchestration.

In WE MD Phase 2, orchestration means:

- intake agent
- task-review agent
- finance-check agent
- summary/reporting agent

OpenAI’s Agents SDK is explicitly designed for specialized agents, handoffs, streaming, and full traces, which matches this multi-step operations pattern. citeturn956612search2turn956612search17

### 3) MCP tools expand
In Phase 2, expand the MCP toolset to include controlled read/write operations:

- `get_pending_tasks`
- `get_overdue_items`
- `get_finance_items_waiting_approval`
- `draft_followup_message`
- `mark_task_status`
- `attach_proof_to_record`
- `generate_weekly_summary`

Because MCP tools act as the model’s operational manual, they need narrow names and clear descriptions. OpenAI explicitly highlights the importance of clear MCP tool definitions for reliability and trust. citeturn956612search16turn956612search23

## WE MD systems to connect in Phase 2

| System | Why it matters now |
|---|---|
| **Task store** | Status changes, due dates, owner tracking |
| **Approval register** | Queue of items awaiting decision |
| **Document store** | Receipts, proofs, notes |
| **Chat interface** | Daily operational use |
| **Reporting layer** | Daily/weekly summaries |

## Human workflow in Phase 2

### Example flow
1. Subha Sister enters: “Money given for school notebooks, receipt will come later.”
2. Agent classifies this as finance-related and flags missing proof.
3. Record is stored with status: `Awaiting proof`.
4. Weekly summary shows:
   - total finance notes
   - missing proofs
   - pending approvals
5. You review only exceptions, not every raw message.

That is a practical use of tool-calling plus orchestration, not “AI replacing management.”

## What still stays human in Phase 2

- actual financial approval
- final sign-off on exception cases
- role/ownership changes
- any external official communication

This matters because OpenAI’s docs make clear that agentic workflows need guardrails, especially around risky tool use. citeturn956612search11turn956612search3

## Outcome of Phase 2

At the end of Phase 2, WE MD gets:

- operational chat interface
- readable task and approval dashboards
- guided follow-up drafting
- structured finance exception visibility
- weekly summary generation

This phase gives **operational control without surrendering authority**.

---

# Phase 3 — Controlled automation and system integration

## Goal of Phase 3

Let the WE MD system do selected actions automatically, but only where the risk is low and the rules are clear.

This is the first phase where the agent becomes an **active operator**, not just a recorder and summarizer.

## What users do in Phase 3

Users can now ask:

- “Send reminder to all owners with overdue tasks”
- “Prepare weekly board-style summary”
- “Route all new finance items to approval queue”
- “Open a missing-proof case for all unresolved finance entries”
- “Show only items blocked for more than 7 days”

## What the system does

The agent can now:

- trigger reminders
- update statuses based on clear rules
- route items to queues automatically
- prepare governance summaries on schedule
- create exception buckets without waiting for manual sorting

This is where **scheduled invocation + agent workflow + MCP tools** really combine well. The scheduler or trigger starts the work, the agent reasons through it, and MCP gives access to the systems. OpenAI’s agent docs, tool docs, and MCP docs all support this style of tool-using workflow. citeturn956612search6turn956612search10turn956612search3

## Practical OpenAI components in Phase 3

### 1) Agents SDK as the main runtime
At this stage the backend is the real system, not just a prototype.

You use the Agents SDK or Responses-based backend to:

- accept scheduled jobs
- process user requests
- call MCP tools
- maintain traces
- support specialized sub-agents

OpenAI’s docs position the Agents SDK for exactly this kind of agentic application with traces and orchestration. citeturn956612search2turn956612search4

### 2) MCP server becomes the operations bridge
By Phase 3 your MCP server could expose tools like:

- `queue_for_approval`
- `send_owner_reminder`
- `generate_board_summary`
- `create_exception_case`
- `fetch_unresolved_finance_items`
- `archive_completed_items`
- `lookup_person_history`

OpenAI’s MCP and connector docs frame remote MCP as the bridge to external capabilities, while tool docs describe remote MCP servers and custom functions as the way to extend the model safely. citeturn956612search3turn956612search10turn956612search19

### 3) Optional ChatGPT-native exposure
Only if useful later, you could expose selected WE MD tools into ChatGPT itself through the Apps SDK / MCP route, so the same operations system can be used from ChatGPT. OpenAI documents building MCP servers and connecting them for ChatGPT app-style integrations. citeturn956612search7turn956612search23

## WE MD systems to connect in Phase 3

| System | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Task system** | Full lifecycle management |
| **Approval engine** | Routing and human sign-off |
| **Document store** | Mandatory proof/evidence handling |
| **Communication tool** | Reminder drafting and dispatch |
| **Summary/report output** | Weekly or monthly governance view |
| **Identity/role map** | Decide who can see or act on what |

## The exact safe automation boundary

### Automate
- classification
- routing
- reminders
- summarization
- queue generation
- missing-proof detection
- overdue detection

### Do not automate without explicit approval
- money release
- official final approvals
- deletion of records
- retroactive correction of finance entries
- sensitive external messages

That boundary is the difference between a useful WE MD operations system and a risky one.

## Outcome of Phase 3

At the end of Phase 3, WE MD gets:

- controlled operational automation
- approval-centered governance
- reliable exception handling
- low-risk delegation to the system
- less dependence on your personal memory and manual chasing

This is where the system starts behaving like an **operations layer**, not just a note-taking assistant.

---

# Visual map: OpenAI stack → WE MD phases

| OpenAI piece | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Phase 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Agent Builder** | Design intake workflow | Refine branching and summaries | Mature workflow versions |
| **ChatKit** | Not essential yet | Main staff interface | Mature operational UI |
| **Responses API / Agents SDK** | Run structured intake | Handle multi-step review flows | Main orchestration runtime |
| **MCP server** | Simple storage tools | Retrieval + controlled updates | Full operations bridge |
| **Tracing / evals** | Check extraction accuracy | Check routing quality | Check automation safety |
| **Approval gating** | Required for all writes | Required for finance/status exceptions | Required for sensitive actions |

This progression matches OpenAI’s documented separation between workflow design, embedded chat, orchestration, external tool access, and safety evaluation. citeturn956612search0turn956612search1turn956612search2turn956612search3turn956612search11

---

# What I would build first for WE MD

## Week-1 practical scope

Not “full agent.”

Just this:

1. one intake agent
2. one MCP server with 4–6 narrow tools
3. one structured storage backend
4. one daily pending-items summary
5. all finance actions read-only except manual review

That is the smallest useful version.

## Example of first 6 MCP tools

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `log_activity` | Save raw operational note |
| `create_task_record` | Store task with owner/status |
| `create_finance_note` | Store finance event without approval |
| `create_approval_request` | Open approval item |
| `get_pending_summary` | Return current pending list |
| `get_missing_proofs` | Return finance entries lacking proof |

This keeps the first version narrow, reviewable, and useful.

---

# Final practical reading

## Phase 1
**Capture and structure.**

## Phase 2
**Review and govern.**

## Phase 3
**Automate selected low-risk operations.**

That is the cleanest way to map OpenAI’s actual stack onto WE MD without hype.

If you want, next I’ll convert this into a **box-and-arrow architecture diagram for WE MD using the exact OpenAI stack names**.

## 27/03/2026 05:28  
Project: AT-MCP-00000-Integration-Exploration  
Page: 00000-05-RealWorld-DataEngineering-Agent-LLM-MCP-ToolFlow  

You’re right. Let’s use a **real stack that companies actually use**, not a made-up thesis.

# Real-world example stack

We’ll take this practical setup:

| Layer | Real tool |
|---|---|
| **Scheduler / orchestration** | Apache Airflow |
| **Agent framework** | OpenAI Responses API or Agents SDK |
| **LLM** | GPT model used through Responses API |
| **Protocol / tool bridge** | MCP server |
| **Warehouse / execution** | Snowflake SQL API |
| **Transformation / data quality** | dbt (`dbt source freshness`) |
| **Notification** | Slack incoming webhook |
| **Incident tracking** | Jira issue API |

Why this is realistic:

- Airflow is built to monitor DAGs and trigger task instances when dependencies are met. citeturn823958search3turn823958search24
- OpenAI’s Responses API is positioned as a unified interface for building agent-like apps with tools, including remote MCP servers. citeturn823958search21turn823958search0
- OpenAI’s Agents SDK is explicitly for agentic applications with tools, handoffs, and traces. citeturn823958search1turn823958search11
- MCP is an open specification for connecting language-model clients to external tools and resources, and the protocol exposes tools, resources, and prompts. citeturn823958search22turn823958search12turn823958search16
- Snowflake’s SQL API can submit SQL statements and check execution status, and Snowflake tasks can run on schedules or events. citeturn393022search9turn393022search17turn393022search1
- dbt provides source freshness checks and supports building downstream models only when sources are fresh enough. citeturn393022search0turn393022search8turn393022search16
- Slack incoming webhooks let apps post JSON payloads to channels, and Jira’s REST API supports creating issues. citeturn393022search2turn393022search18turn393022search3turn393022search7

---

# The business problem

A company has a daily **sales data pipeline**:

```text
ERP / app database
   ↓
Ingestion
   ↓
Snowflake raw tables
   ↓
dbt models
   ↓
BI dashboard
```

Every morning, the company wants to know:

> “Did yesterday’s sales pipeline finish correctly?  
> If not, where did it break, how serious is it, and who should act?”

This is exactly the type of workflow where **Scheduler → AI Agent → LLM → MCP → other systems** becomes useful. citeturn823958search3turn823958search1turn823958search22

---

# Step 1 — What the scheduler does

In this stack, **Airflow** is the scheduler/orchestrator of the data pipeline itself. Airflow documentation says the scheduler monitors DAGs and triggers task instances once dependencies are complete. It also supports event-driven scheduling in newer versions, so a workflow can run because of time or because an external event arrives. citeturn823958search3turn823958search17turn823958search20

## Practical Airflow role

At **07:00 every day**, Airflow runs a DAG like:

```text
sales_pipeline_monitor
```

That DAG may do three things:

1. Check whether ingestion finished
2. Check whether dbt freshness/tests look healthy
3. Trigger an AI-based incident-investigation step only if something is wrong

At this point, Airflow is **not the AI agent**. It is just the **time/event trigger plus workflow runner**. That’s the key difference. citeturn823958search3turn823958search17

---

# Step 2 — What the AI agent does

Now the Airflow DAG calls an **agent service** built with the OpenAI Responses API or the OpenAI Agents SDK. OpenAI’s docs describe the Responses API as a unified way to build agent-like apps with built-in tools and remote MCPs, and the Agents SDK as a way to build agentic apps with tools, handoffs, and full traces. citeturn823958search21turn823958search1

## Practical agent goal

Airflow passes a goal such as:

```json
{
  "pipeline": "sales_daily",
  "business_date": "2026-03-26",
  "trigger_reason": "freshness_failed"
}
```

The **AI agent** then owns the task:

- investigate what failed
- gather evidence
- classify severity
- notify the right people
- create a Jira incident if needed

So here:

- **Airflow** = starts the work
- **AI agent** = manages the investigation workflow

That is a real separation of responsibilities, not theory. citeturn823958search3turn823958search1turn823958search11

---

# Step 3 — Where the LLM fits

Inside that agent, the **LLM** is the reasoning engine.

OpenAI’s tool docs describe tools and remote MCPs as extensions to the model’s capabilities, while the Responses API supports multi-turn reasoning and tool use. In practice, that means the model can inspect evidence, decide what to check next, and turn technical details into a readable explanation. citeturn823958search4turn823958search21turn823958search0

## Example

Suppose the agent receives this raw signal:

```text
dbt source freshness failed for source: sales_orders
max_loaded_at = 2026-03-26 03:05:00
error_after = 2 hours
current_time = 2026-03-26 07:00:00
```

dbt’s source freshness feature is specifically meant to measure how recent the newest record is, compared with now, and it supports warning/error thresholds. citeturn393022search4turn393022search0

The LLM can turn that into:

> “The source appears stale by nearly two hours beyond the configured threshold, so downstream models may produce incomplete sales reporting.”

That interpretation layer is what the LLM adds. The scheduler does not do this. The protocol does not do this. The warehouse does not do this. citeturn393022search4turn823958search21

---

# Step 4 — Where MCP fits

Now comes the part you specifically asked for.

**MCP is not the LLM and not the agent.** MCP is the standard bridge that lets the model/client connect to external tools and resources in a structured way. The MCP specification describes servers exposing tools, resources, and prompts. OpenAI’s docs also explain remote MCP servers as a way to give models new capabilities and connect them to outside services, with approval controls if the developer wants that. citeturn823958search22turn823958search12turn823958search16turn823958search0

## In this real stack, the MCP server can expose tools like:

- `get_airflow_run_status`
- `read_dbt_artifact`
- `run_snowflake_sql`
- `post_slack_message`
- `create_jira_issue`

So the agent does **not** hardcode 20 different custom integrations into the prompt. Instead, it asks for tools through MCP. That is the practical value of MCP. citeturn823958search14turn823958search22turn823958search16

---

# Step 5 — Concrete end-to-end flow

Now let’s walk through a full real-world incident.

## Scenario

Yesterday’s sales dashboard is low.

The actual issue: source ingestion stalled, so Snowflake raw data is incomplete, dbt freshness failed, and downstream marts should not be trusted.

---

## Step 5.1 — Airflow triggers the monitor job

Airflow runs at **07:00** and notices the validation path needs investigation. Airflow is doing what its docs say it does: monitoring workflows and triggering tasks according to schedule/dependencies. citeturn823958search3turn823958search24

Example DAG branch:

```python
if freshness_status == "failed":
    trigger_ai_investigation()
```

---

## Step 5.2 — Agent starts with a goal

The agent receives:

```json
{
  "pipeline": "sales_daily",
  "date": "2026-03-26",
  "symptom": "dbt freshness failure"
}
```

Because the agent is built with Responses API / Agents SDK, it can keep context across turns and use tools. That is exactly the type of workflow OpenAI documents these systems for. citeturn823958search21turn823958search1

---

## Step 5.3 — Agent asks MCP for dbt evidence

The agent calls an MCP tool:

```json
{
  "tool": "read_dbt_artifact",
  "args": {
    "job": "sales_dbt_prod",
    "artifact": "sources.json"
  }
}
```

This is realistic because MCP servers expose tools, and dbt artifacts plus source freshness are standard things to inspect in production workflows. dbt’s docs say `dbt source freshness` checks freshness, and you can build downstream models based on source freshness status. citeturn823958search16turn393022search0turn393022search8

Returned result:

```json
{
  "source_name": "sales_orders",
  "status": "error",
  "max_loaded_at": "2026-03-26T03:05:00Z",
  "error_after_hours": 2
}
```

---

## Step 5.4 — LLM interprets the dbt result

The LLM reasons:

- last source data arrived at 03:05
- by 07:00 it is older than policy
- dashboard based on this source may be incomplete

This is the **LLM** step: interpretation, not system access. That separation matters. citeturn393022search4turn823958search21

---

## Step 5.5 — Agent asks MCP to query Snowflake

The agent now needs proof from the warehouse.

MCP tool call:

```json
{
  "tool": "run_snowflake_sql",
  "args": {
    "sql": "select count(*) as cnt from raw.sales_orders where order_date = '2026-03-26';"
  }
}
```

Snowflake’s SQL API is built exactly for this kind of integration: submitting statements and checking execution status programmatically. citeturn393022search9turn393022search17

Suppose result:

```json
{
  "cnt": 128944
}
```

Then the agent checks yesterday’s normal pattern:

```json
{
  "tool": "run_snowflake_sql",
  "args": {
    "sql": "select order_date, count(*) as cnt from raw.sales_orders where order_date between '2026-03-20' and '2026-03-26' group by 1 order by 1;"
  }
}
```

Result:

```text
2026-03-20  410221
2026-03-21  425090
2026-03-22  398101
2026-03-23  441330
2026-03-24  436902
2026-03-25  448710
2026-03-26  128944
```

Now the agent has evidence that the current day is abnormally low.

---

## Step 5.6 — Agent checks whether ingestion was event-triggered or time-triggered

This is where scheduler and eventing matter.

Airflow supports event-driven scheduling as well as time-based scheduling, and Snowflake tasks can also be scheduled or triggered by events like new data arriving in a stream. citeturn823958search17turn393022search1

If the company uses a Snowflake task or upstream event to continue processing, the agent can inspect whether the expected trigger happened.

MCP call:

```json
{
  "tool": "run_snowflake_sql",
  "args": {
    "sql": "show tasks like 'sales_ingest_%';"
  }
}
```

Or an MCP tool might wrap that into:

```json
{
  "tool": "get_ingestion_task_status",
  "args": {
    "pipeline": "sales_daily"
  }
}
```

If the task did not fire, that points to orchestration.  
If it fired but data is still low, that points to source or load failure.

---

## Step 5.7 — Agent asks LLM for diagnosis

Now the LLM gets a full evidence bundle:

- dbt freshness failed
- Snowflake row count is far below baseline
- ingestion trigger/task status abnormal or incomplete

The LLM can now produce something like:

> “The most likely root cause is delayed or incomplete ingestion into raw.sales_orders. dbt freshness failure is a symptom, not the root cause. Downstream marts should be treated as stale until ingestion completes and dbt is rerun.”

That is a real use of the LLM: synthesis across tools. citeturn823958search21turn823958search4

---

# Step 6 — Agent takes action through MCP into other systems

Now the investigation is done.  
The system has to **act**.

This is where “other systems” become visible.

---

## Step 6.1 — Post to Slack

Slack incoming webhooks accept a JSON payload sent to a unique URL tied to a channel. Slack’s docs say you can format messages and use layout blocks, and webhook posting has rate limits around 1 per second with short bursts allowed. citeturn393022search2turn393022search18turn393022search22

MCP call:

```json
{
  "tool": "post_slack_message",
  "args": {
    "channel": "#data-ops",
    "text": "Sales pipeline alert: dbt freshness failed for 2026-03-26. Raw row count is 128,944 vs normal ~400k+. Dashboard may be incomplete."
  }
}
```

That MCP tool would typically wrap Slack webhook logic underneath.

---

## Step 6.2 — Create a Jira incident

Atlassian’s Jira REST API supports issue operations including creating issues. citeturn393022search3turn393022search7

MCP call:

```json
{
  "tool": "create_jira_issue",
  "args": {
    "project": "DE",
    "issue_type": "Incident",
    "summary": "sales_daily stale on 2026-03-26 due to incomplete ingestion",
    "description": "dbt freshness failed for source sales_orders; Snowflake raw count was 128,944 vs normal ~400k+; downstream marts should be rerun after source recovery."
  }
}
```

Again, the agent does not need Jira API details in the prompt. MCP standardizes the tool interface. citeturn823958search22turn823958search16turn393022search3

---

## Step 6.3 — Optionally trigger recovery logic

This part is where companies must be careful.

Snowflake tasks can automate data processing and can be scheduled or event-triggered, but allowing an agent to actually restart production jobs is a governance decision, not just a technical one. OpenAI’s MCP/connectors docs explicitly note that tool calls can be auto-allowed or gated behind explicit approval. citeturn393022search1turn823958search0

So a safe design is:

- **AI agent can investigate**
- **AI agent can notify**
- **AI agent can draft the remediation**
- **Human approves rerun / backfill / destructive action**

That is usually the right production pattern. citeturn823958search0turn823958search1

---

# Same flow in one clean chain

## 1) Scheduler
**Airflow** runs the monitor DAG on time or event. citeturn823958search3turn823958search17

## 2) AI Agent
An agent built with **OpenAI Responses API / Agents SDK** receives the investigation goal and manages the sequence. citeturn823958search21turn823958search1

## 3) LLM
The model interprets dbt freshness output, SQL results, and incident context into a diagnosis. citeturn393022search4turn823958search21

## 4) MCP
The model/client reaches external capabilities through an **MCP server**, which exposes tools/resources/prompts in a standard way. citeturn823958search22turn823958search12turn823958search16

## 5) Other systems
The MCP tools interact with **dbt, Snowflake, Slack, Jira, Airflow**, and possibly more systems like docs or runbooks. citeturn393022search0turn393022search9turn393022search2turn393022search3turn823958search3

---

# Why this is better than “LLM directly talks to everything”

Because in real companies:

- systems are many
- credentials are sensitive
- actions need guardrails
- context has to persist across tools
- approval rules matter

MCP gives a standardized tool layer, OpenAI’s agent stack gives orchestration and reasoning, and enterprise tools remain the actual systems of record. That separation is exactly why MCP exists and why OpenAI documents remote MCP servers as a structured extension path instead of stuffing everything into one monolithic prompt. citeturn823958search22turn823958search0turn823958search14

---

# Practical difference in one line each

| Thing | Real job |
|---|---|
| **Airflow** | Starts the process |
| **Agent** | Runs the investigation workflow |
| **LLM** | Understands and explains |
| **MCP** | Gives standard controlled access to tools |
| **Snowflake/dbt/Slack/Jira** | Do the real operational work |

This is the cleanest real-world explanation. citeturn823958search3turn823958search1turn823958search22turn393022search9turn393022search0turn393022search2turn393022search3

---

# What a company would actually build first

A realistic first version would be:

1. Airflow runs validation every morning. citeturn823958search3
2. dbt source freshness is checked first. citeturn393022search0turn393022search16
3. If freshness/test fails, an OpenAI agent is called. citeturn823958search21turn823958search1

# Short Answer

> ❌ **No — I (the model) am NOT this app**  
> ✅ This app is just **one interface to access me**

---

# Clear Separation

## 1. This App (what you are using now)

This is:

- ChatGPT interface (web / mobile)
- UI + chat experience
- includes:
  - chat window
  - memory
  - tools (sometimes)
  - settings

👉 Think:

> **App = Door**

---

## 2. Me (what you are talking to)

I am:

- GPT model (LLM)
- accessed through API or app
- same “brain” can be used in:
  - this app
  - your own backend
  - agent systems
  - other products

👉 Think:

> **Me = Brain**

---

## 3. Full Picture

```text
ChatGPT App (UI)
        ↓
OpenAI API (Responses API)
        ↓
👉 GPT Model (ME)
        ↓
Tools / MCP / Systems (if used)
```

---

# Why this confusion happens

Because in this app:

- UI + Model feel like one thing
- You type → I reply instantly

So it feels like:

> “ChatGPT = AI”

But actually:

| Layer | Reality |
|---|---|
| App | Interface |
| API | Access layer |
| Model (me) | Intelligence |

---

# Example to make it clear

## Same “me” can exist in:

- This ChatGPT app ✅  
- Your own company system ✅  
- A WhatsApp bot ✅  
- A data engineering agent ✅  
- A voice assistant ✅  

👉 Only the **interface changes**  
👉 The **brain remains the same type**

---

# Analogy (simple)

| Thing | Real-world |
|---|---|
| ChatGPT App | Phone 📱 |
| Me (model) | Person you call 👤 |
| API | Network connection 📡 |

---

# Important Insight (for your direction)

Right now:

```text
You → ChatGPT App → Me → Answer
```

Future (your system):

```text
User / Trigger
→ Your Agent (backend)
→ Me (via API)
→ MCP tools
→ Systems
→ Output
```

---

# Final one-line clarity

> **ChatGPT app = interface**  
> **Me = intelligence behind it**

---

If you want next:

👉 I can show **how you call “me” from your own system (step-by-step API flow)**  
That is the exact bridge from learning → building.

Yes. Here is a **full practical Python example** for:

```text
audio file
→ transcript
→ summary
→ task extraction
→ store as JSON
→ notify by email
```

OpenAI’s current docs recommend the **Responses API** for new text-generation projects, the Python SDK is `pip install openai`, and the speech-to-text docs show using the transcription endpoint with models like `gpt-4o-transcribe` / `gpt-4o-mini-transcribe`. The quickstart currently shows `gpt-5.4` as the flagship text model example. citeturn113319search3turn113319search4turn993475search0turn993475search15

---

# What this example does

## Input
- `meeting.m4a` or `call.wav`

## Output
- raw transcript text
- clean summary
- extracted action items
- saved JSON file
- email notification

---

# Install

```bash
pip install openai
```

The official SDK install command is `pip install openai`, and the API key is typically provided through the `OPENAI_API_KEY` environment variable. citeturn113319search3turn993475search5turn993475search10

Set your key:

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY="your_api_key_here"
```

---

# Full Python script

```python
import os
import json
import smtplib
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.mime.text import MIMEText
from email.mime.multipart import MIMEMultipart
from typing import Any, Dict, List

from openai import OpenAI


# =========================
# CONFIG
# =========================

OPENAI_TEXT_MODEL = "gpt-5.4"
OPENAI_TRANSCRIBE_MODEL = "gpt-4o-mini-transcribe"

AUDIO_FILE = "meeting.m4a"  # change to your file

OUTPUT_DIR = Path("output")
OUTPUT_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# Email notification config
SMTP_HOST = "smtp.gmail.com"
SMTP_PORT = 587
SMTP_USERNAME = os.getenv("SMTP_USERNAME", "")
SMTP_PASSWORD = os.getenv("SMTP_PASSWORD", "")
EMAIL_FROM = os.getenv("EMAIL_FROM", "")
EMAIL_TO = os.getenv("EMAIL_TO", "")

client = OpenAI()


# =========================
# STEP 1: TRANSCRIBE AUDIO
# =========================

def transcribe_audio(audio_path: str) -> str:
    """
    Transcribe an audio file using OpenAI's transcription API.
    """
    with open(audio_path, "rb") as f:
        transcript = client.audio.transcriptions.create(
            model=OPENAI_TRANSCRIBE_MODEL,
            file=f,
        )

    # Depending on SDK response shape, text is usually available here.
    # Keep this tolerant in case the SDK object changes shape slightly.
    text = getattr(transcript, "text", None)
    if not text:
        raise RuntimeError("Transcription returned no text.")
    return text


# =========================================
# STEP 2: SUMMARIZE + EXTRACT TASKS IN JSON
# =========================================

def analyze_transcript(transcript_text: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Ask the model for a summary + action items in strict JSON format.
    """
    prompt = f"""
You are an operations analyst.

Read the transcript below and return ONLY valid JSON with this exact shape:

{{
  "title": "short title",
  "summary": "3-8 sentence summary",
  "participants": ["name1", "name2"],
  "key_points": ["point 1", "point 2"],
  "action_items": [
    {{
      "task": "what needs to be done",
      "owner": "person name or Unknown",
      "due_date": "ISO date if explicit, else null",
      "priority": "high|medium|low",
      "status": "open"
    }}
  ],
  "risks": ["risk 1", "risk 2"],
  "follow_ups_needed": true
}}

Rules:
- Return JSON only. No markdown.
- If owner is unclear, use "Unknown".
- If due date is unclear, use null.
- Do not invent facts not present in the transcript.
- If there are no action items, return an empty list.

Transcript:
\"\"\"
{transcript_text}
\"\"\"
"""

    response = client.responses.create(
        model=OPENAI_TEXT_MODEL,
        input=prompt,
    )

    raw = response.output_text.strip()

    try:
        return json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        # Save the raw response for debugging
        debug_file = OUTPUT_DIR / "bad_model_output.txt"
        debug_file.write_text(raw, encoding="utf-8")
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"Model output was not valid JSON. Saved raw output to {debug_file}"
        ) from e


# =========================
# STEP 3: STORE RESULTS
# =========================

def store_results(audio_path: str, transcript_text: str, analysis: Dict[str, Any]) -> Path:
    """
    Save everything into one JSON file.
    """
    timestamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ")
    stem = Path(audio_path).stem

    payload = {
        "created_at_utc": timestamp,
        "source_audio_file": audio_path,
        "transcript": transcript_text,
        "analysis": analysis,
    }

    output_file = OUTPUT_DIR / f"{stem}_{timestamp}.json"
    output_file.write_text(json.dumps(payload, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")
    return output_file


# =========================
# STEP 4: EMAIL NOTIFY
# =========================

def send_email_notification(result_file: Path, analysis: Dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    """
    Send a simple email summary.
    """
    if not all([SMTP_USERNAME, SMTP_PASSWORD, EMAIL_FROM, EMAIL_TO]):
        print("Email config not set. Skipping notification.")
        return

    subject = f"[Transcript Processed] {analysis.get('title', 'Untitled')}"
    summary = analysis.get("summary", "")
    action_items: List[Dict[str, Any]] = analysis.get("action_items", [])

    lines = [
        f"Result file: {result_file}",
        "",
        "Summary:",
        summary,
        "",
        "Action Items:",
    ]

    if action_items:
        for idx, item in enumerate(action_items, start=1):
            lines.append(
                f"{idx}. Task: {item.get('task')} | "
                f"Owner: {item.get('owner')} | "
                f"Due: {item.get('due_date')} | "
                f"Priority: {item.get('priority')}"
            )
    else:
        lines.append("No action items found.")

    body = "\n".join(lines)

    msg = MIMEMultipart()
    msg["From"] = EMAIL_FROM
    msg["To"] = EMAIL_TO
    msg["Subject"] = subject
    msg.attach(MIMEText(body, "plain", "utf-8"))

    with smtplib.SMTP(SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT) as server:
        server.starttls()
        server.login(SMTP_USERNAME, SMTP_PASSWORD)
        server.sendmail(EMAIL_FROM, [EMAIL_TO], msg.as_string())

    print(f"Notification sent to {EMAIL_TO}")


# =========================
# MAIN
# =========================

def main() -> None:
    print(f"Transcribing: {AUDIO_FILE}")
    transcript_text = transcribe_audio(AUDIO_FILE)

    transcript_file = OUTPUT_DIR / "transcript.txt"
    transcript_file.write_text(transcript_text, encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"Transcript saved to {transcript_file}")

    print("Analyzing transcript...")
    analysis = analyze_transcript(transcript_text)

    result_file = store_results(AUDIO_FILE, transcript_text, analysis)
    print(f"Structured result saved to {result_file}")

    send_email_notification(result_file, analysis)

    print("\nDone.")
    print(json.dumps(analysis, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```json
    "summary": "The team reviewed pending donor follow-ups and account-opening status...",
    "participants": ["Senthil", "Subha"],
    "key_points": [
      "Bank account opening is still pending",
      "Receipt proof is missing for one item"
    ],
    "action_items": [
      {
        "task": "Follow up with the bank manager",
        "owner": "Subha",
        "due_date": null,
        "priority": "high",
        "status": "open"
      }
    ],
    "risks": [
      "Delay in account setup may block donations"
    ],
    "follow_ups_needed": true
  }
}
```

---

# How the flow works

## 1. `client.audio.transcriptions.create(...)`
This sends the audio file to the transcription endpoint. OpenAI’s speech-to-text docs list supported input formats including `mp3`, `mp4`, `m4a`, `wav`, and `webm`, and note a current file upload limit of 25 MB for standard transcription requests. citeturn993475search0turn993475search8

## 2. `client.responses.create(...)`
This sends the transcript text to the Responses API for summarization and task extraction. OpenAI currently recommends the Responses API for new projects and positions it as the main text-generation interface for agent-like applications. citeturn113319search4turn113319search8turn113319search1

## 3. JSON store
This example stores results locally in a JSON file. In a real product, you would usually swap this with:
- PostgreSQL
- Google Sheets
- Airtable
- Notion
- internal task database

## 4. notify
This example uses SMTP email only because it is easy to understand. In a product, this could instead be:
- Slack webhook
- Teams message
- WhatsApp provider
- task-system update

---

# Real improvements for production

## Better than this demo
This script is practical, but for production I would add:

- chunking for long transcripts
- retry logic
- schema validation
- cost logging
- speaker diarization
- deduplication
- queue/job processing
- database storage instead of flat JSON
- Slack/Jira notification instead of plain email

OpenAI’s current audio docs also include diarization-capable transcription models, and the Responses API supports tool-using, multi-step patterns if you later want to turn this into a fuller agent workflow. citeturn993475search0turn113319search4turn113319search10

---

# If you want speaker names too

Use a diarization-capable transcription model and return speaker segments first, then feed that cleaner transcript into the summarization step. The speech-to-text docs list `gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize` for diarized output. citeturn993475search0

---

# Minimum folder structure

```text
your_project/
  app.py
  output/
  .env   # optional, if you load env vars this way
```

---

# Very small test version

If you want to test only summary + task extraction from an existing transcript file, use this smaller function:

```python
from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI()

transcript_text = open("transcript.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8").read()

response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-5.4",
    input=f"Summarize and extract action items as JSON from this transcript:\n\n{transcript_text}"
)

print(response.output_text)
```

The official quickstart shows this same basic Python pattern: `client = OpenAI()` followed by `client.responses.create(...)` and then reading `response.output_text`. citeturn113319search3turn113319search0

---

# One practical warning

Because this example asks the model to emit JSON as plain text, it is possible for malformed JSON to happen occasionally. For a production system, use stricter output validation and retries. OpenAI’s docs also provide a Structured Outputs path specifically to enforce JSON-schema-shaped responses. citeturn113319search12

If you want, next I’ll show the **same pipeline upgraded to production style with PostgreSQL + Slack + retry handling**.

Page: 00000-06-Where-to-Setup-OpenAI-Agent-and-UseCases  

You can set up an OpenAI-based agent in **five practical places**, depending on what you want it to do. OpenAI’s current stack separates **building** from **deploying**: Agent Builder is the visual canvas for creating multi-step workflows; Responses API is the lower-level API recommended for new agent-like applications; Agents SDK is the higher-level framework for orchestration; ChatKit is for embedding agent chat into your own product; and the Apps SDK is for building apps that extend ChatGPT itself. citeturn537312view0turn537312view3turn608284view3turn259771search5turn583623view3

# 1. Where to set up the agent

## Option A — Inside **Agent Builder** first

This is the best place to **design** the workflow. OpenAI describes Agent Builder as a visual canvas where you assemble, debug, and export multi-step agent workflows, using nodes, typed inputs and outputs, live preview, and versioned publishing. The documented build flow is: **design workflow → publish workflow → deploy workflow**. citeturn537312view3

### Use this when
- you want to sketch the logic before writing much code
- you want to test routing between steps
- you want a versioned workflow ID you can later deploy elsewhere citeturn537312view3

### Step by step
1. Open Agent Builder.
2. Create a workflow with nodes.
3. Add agents, tools, and control flow.
4. Test it in Preview with sample inputs.
5. Publish it to get a workflow version.
6. Then either embed it with ChatKit or export code for your own stack. citeturn537312view3

---

## Option B — Inside **your own product UI** with **ChatKit**

If you already have a website or internal app and want a chat-style agent inside it, ChatKit is OpenAI’s recommended path. OpenAI says ChatKit lets you embed a workflow into your application by passing the workflow ID, and the quickstart includes creating a ChatKit session, generating a client secret on your backend, and embedding the chat frontend in your product. citeturn259771search0turn259771search2turn259771search5

### Use this when
- you want employees or customers to use the agent in your app
- you want chat UI without building the full front end yourself
- you want faster deployment than fully custom infrastructure citeturn259771search0turn259771search2

### Step by step
1. Build the workflow in Agent Builder.
2. Publish it and get the workflow ID.
3. Create a backend endpoint that creates ChatKit sessions.
4. Pass a unique user ID from your backend for each signed-in user.
5. Hand the client secret to the ChatKit frontend.
6. Embed the chat widget in your site.
7. Customize appearance later if needed. citeturn259771search0turn259771search6

---

## Option C — In **your own backend/server** with the **Agents SDK**

This is the right place when you want more control. OpenAI says the Agents SDK is meant for agentic applications where a model can use extra context and tools, hand off to specialized agents, stream partial results, and keep a full trace of what happened. OpenAI also says that if you want to get started quickly or build networks of agents, the Agents SDK is the recommended higher-level abstraction, while Responses API gives more control under the hood. citeturn537312view1turn537312view0

### Use this when
- you want custom orchestration
- you need your own auth, policies, or infrastructure
- you want multiple specialized agents working together
- you need traces and deeper control than plain prompting citeturn537312view1turn537312view0

### Step by step
1. Define the main job of the agent.
2. Decide the tools it can call.
3. Build the workflow in code with the Agents SDK.
4. Connect built-in tools or your own functions.
5. Add MCP servers or connectors if external systems are needed.
6. Test with real inputs.
7. Add guardrails and approvals.
8. Deploy on your own backend or alongside ChatKit. citeturn537312view1turn537312view2turn259771search1

---

## Option D — As a **ChatGPT app** with the **Apps SDK + MCP server**

If you want the agent to live **inside ChatGPT itself**, this is the path. OpenAI’s Apps SDK is explicitly described as a way to **build apps to extend ChatGPT**, and the deployment flow includes setting up your server, building your ChatGPT UI, authenticating users, deploying the app, and connecting it from ChatGPT. The “Connect from ChatGPT” guide says you can expose your app through an HTTPS MCP endpoint, create a connector in ChatGPT, and then use it in conversations. citeturn583623view3turn583623view1turn583623view2

### Use this when
- you want the user to access your tool from ChatGPT
- you want tool discovery in ChatGPT
- your app is naturally “ask the assistant, then call my system” citeturn583623view1turn608284view0

### Step by step
1. Build an MCP server reachable over HTTPS.
2. Expose tools with clear names and descriptions.
3. Turn on developer mode in ChatGPT.
4. Go to Settings → Connectors → Create.
5. Enter connector metadata and your `/mcp` endpoint.
6. Test it in a new chat.
7. Refresh metadata whenever tools change.
8. Later publish the app more broadly if needed. citeturn583623view1

---

## Option E — As a **voice agent** with **Realtime API + Agents SDK**

For spoken conversation, OpenAI’s voice-agents guide says the main architectures are speech-to-speech via the Realtime API or chained audio-to-text-to-audio. OpenAI explicitly lists use cases such as **customer support** and **language tutoring**, and recommends the TypeScript Agents SDK as the starting point if you are new to building voice agents. citeturn608284view1turn330168search9

### Use this when
- the user should talk instead of type
- latency matters
- the use case is conversational and interactive citeturn608284view1

### Step by step
1. Pick speech-to-speech or chained architecture.
2. Set up the realtime connection.
3. Create a realtime session.
4. Use a model with audio input/output support.
5. Add tools and context.
6. Test interruption, turn-taking, and error recovery.
7. Deploy in browser, mobile, or server-assisted flow. citeturn608284view1

---

## Option F — As a **UI-operating agent** with **computer use**

If the job is “use a website or desktop-like UI the way a human would,” OpenAI’s computer-use guide gives three paths: the built-in computer-use loop, a custom browser/VM harness such as Playwright or Selenium, or a code-execution harness. OpenAI explicitly describes tasks like navigating a site, filling out a form, and stepping through a multistage workflow. citeturn608284view2

### Use this when
- the target system has no clean API
- the work is naturally done by clicking through UI
- you need the model to inspect screenshots and decide next actions citeturn608284view2

### Step by step
1. Send a plain-language task with the computer tool enabled.
2. Read the returned structured UI actions.
3. Execute those actions in your browser or VM harness.
4. Send back a fresh screenshot.
5. Repeat until the model stops asking for actions.
6. Add human approval for risky steps. citeturn608284view2

---

# 2. So where should **you** set it up?

For your style of work, there are really **three tiers**.

## Tier 1 — Fastest and safest start
Build the logic in **Agent Builder**, then embed it with **ChatKit** if you want people to use it in a product UI. OpenAI explicitly recommends ChatKit if you are unsure which deployment path to choose. citeturn537312view3turn259771search2

## Tier 2 — More serious internal system
Use **Responses API + Agents SDK** in your own backend when you need system control, custom flows, approvals, or multiple agents. OpenAI’s docs position Responses as the recommended primitive for new projects and the Agents SDK as the higher-level orchestration framework built for agentic applications. citeturn608284view3turn537312view0turn537312view1

## Tier 3 — If you want ChatGPT itself to call your system
Build an **Apps SDK / MCP app** so the tools show up inside ChatGPT. That is the right answer when the user experience is “ask ChatGPT, and ChatGPT calls our app.” citeturn583623view3turn583623view1

---

# 3. What use cases does OpenAI’s stack appear to be built for?

I cannot honestly tell you what OpenAI people privately “thought in their heads,” but from the official docs, the intended use-case families are pretty visible.

## A. **Embedded agent experiences inside products**
OpenAI’s deployment docs revolve around embedding workflows into your own frontend with ChatKit, including theming, widgets, actions, and advanced integration. That points strongly to productized in-app assistants, not just demos. citeturn259771search0turn259771search5turn259771search6turn259771search10turn259771search11

### Typical examples
- customer-facing assistant inside a SaaS app
- internal operations assistant for employees
- domain-specific chat over business workflows
- agent-driven UI with buttons, lists, and actions citeturn259771search5turn259771search10turn259771search11

---

## B. **Tool-using agents**
The Responses API and MCP docs emphasize tool use: web search, file search, computer use, code interpreter, remote MCP servers, and custom functions. That makes the platform clearly suited for agents that must do more than answer text. citeturn608284view3turn537312view2turn608284view4

### Typical examples
- search and summarize external information
- inspect uploaded files
- write and run code
- call business systems through MCP
- chain multiple tool calls inside one request citeturn608284view3turn537312view2

---

## C. **Voice agents**
OpenAI explicitly calls out **customer support** and **language tutoring** as voice-agent examples, and also mentions conversational search/discovery and interactive customer service scenarios. citeturn608284view1turn330168search9

### Typical examples
- call center assistant
- educational tutor
- spoken onboarding helper
- voice front desk for a business
- live support for users who do not want typing citeturn608284view1

---

## D. **UI automation / browser-driving agents**
The computer-use guide is clearly aimed at agents that operate interfaces visually, such as navigating websites, filling forms, and completing multistage workflows. citeturn608284view2

### Typical examples
- operate legacy back-office tools
- fill and submit forms
- collect information from a UI
- perform repetitive browser tasks
- guide or partially automate manual workflows citeturn608284view2

---

## E. **Apps that extend ChatGPT**
The Apps SDK docs are very explicit: this part of the stack is for building apps that extend ChatGPT, and the planning docs say discovery is model-driven, depending on your tool metadata, descriptions, and how well the app matches user prompts and memories. citeturn583623view3turn608284view0

### Typical examples
- task board app in ChatGPT
- CRM lookup app in ChatGPT
- internal dashboard app in ChatGPT
- project or approval system exposed as ChatGPT tools
- workflow launcher from a chat prompt citeturn608284view0turn583623view1

---

## F. **Multi-agent orchestration**
OpenAI’s docs repeatedly talk about workflows, orchestration, handoffs to specialized agents, and networks of agents. That suggests a serious target use case is not just “one chatbot,” but **specialized cooperating agents**. citeturn537312view0turn537312view1turn537312view3

### Typical examples
- intake agent → classifier agent → executor agent
- research agent → summarizer agent → notifier agent
- support triage agent → knowledge agent → ticketing agent
- planning agent → approver agent → reporting agent citeturn537312view1turn537312view3

---

# 4. Practical step-by-step: how a company would build one properly

## Phase 1 — Pick the job
OpenAI’s Apps SDK planning guide says successful apps start with a crisp understanding of what the user is trying to accomplish. It recommends gathering user interviews, support requests, prompt samples, and system constraints before defining tools. citeturn608284view0

### What to do
1. Choose one narrow job.
2. Write the exact user asks you want recognized.
3. List direct asks and indirect asks.
4. Identify data sources and compliance constraints. citeturn608284view0

---

## Phase 2 — Define tools
After the use case is clear, define the tools the agent may use. OpenAI’s docs center the stack around models, tools, state/memory, and orchestration, and the MCP/connectors docs show how remote MCP servers and connectors extend the model’s capabilities. citeturn537312view0turn537312view2

### What to do
1. List all systems the agent needs.
2. Separate read tools from write tools.
3. Add approvals for risky actions.
4. Keep tool descriptions very clear. citeturn537312view2turn608284view0

---

## Phase 3 — Build the workflow
You can do this visually in Agent Builder or directly in code with the Agents SDK / Responses API. OpenAI’s own recommendation is Agent Builder for visual workflow design and ChatKit if you are not sure how to deploy. citeturn537312view3turn259771search2

### What to do
1. Add the main agent.
2. Add specialized nodes or tools.
3. Define branching logic.
4. Test with live or sample inputs.
5. Publish a version. citeturn537312view3

---

## Phase 4 — Choose deployment
At this point, choose one of the deployment homes:
- **ChatKit** for embedding in your app,
- **custom backend with Agents SDK** for deeper control,
- **Apps SDK + MCP** for ChatGPT-native usage,
- **Realtime + Agents SDK** for voice,
- **computer use** for UI-driven jobs. citeturn259771search5turn537312view1turn583623view1turn608284view1turn608284view2

---

## Phase 5 — Add safety and approvals
OpenAI’s docs repeatedly point to safety risks in agent workflows and note that MCP/connectors tool calls can be auto-allowed or gated behind explicit approval by the developer. citeturn537312view3turn537312view2

### What to do
1. Require human confirmation for money movement, deletion, production changes, or customer-facing writes.
2. Treat screenshots, PDFs, emails, and third-party content as untrusted input.
3. Restrict tools by scope and role. citeturn537312view2turn608284view2

---

## Phase 6 — Iterate with traces and evals
The stack is not only for building agents; it also includes trace grading and eval tools for improving them. Agent Builder supports evaluation over traces, and the Agents pages point to evals, datasets, and prompt optimization. citeturn537312view3turn259771search5

### What to do
1. Save traces.
2. Review failures.
3. Add tests for frequent scenarios.
4. Tune prompts, tools, and routing. citeturn537312view3turn259771search5

---

Below is the broadest honest list I can infer from the official docs and the product structure.

## Internal operations
- task assistant
- approval assistant
- incident triage
- knowledge retrieval
- document Q&A
- status reporting
- workflow launcher

- internal voice helpdesk citeturn537312view0turn537312view2turn608284view1turn608284view2

## Customer-facing product use
- support chat
- onboarding assistant

- multilingual voice support citeturn608284view1turn259771search5

- homework helper
- guided practice

- feedback assistant citeturn608284view1turn537312view3

- policy lookup assistant
- contract or report extraction
- multi-document investigation assistant citeturn608284view3turn608284view4

## Developer and technical workflows
- coding assistant
- code-running helper
- debugging workflow with tools
- multi-step engineering investigation
- custom product support bot with traces and evals citeturn608284view3turn537312view1turn259771search5

## ChatGPT-native apps
- Jira-style task connector
- kanban board assistant

# 6. For your own system, the best starting point

For **WE MD / approvals / task tracking / financial visibility**, I would not start with a general “do anything” agent. I would start with a **narrow internal operations agent** on your own backend using **Responses API + Agents SDK**, and only expose read-heavy tools first. That matches OpenAI’s documented architecture split: Responses for new agent-like projects, Agents SDK for orchestration, and MCP/connectors for external systems. citeturn608284view3turn537312view0turn537312view2

A safe first rollout would be:
1. intake and classify messages,
2. create structured tasks,
3. fetch status from systems,
4. draft summaries,
5. require approval for any write action. OpenAI’s tooling model supports this because MCP calls can be approval-gated, and agent workflows are explicitly built around tools plus orchestration. citeturn537312view2turn537312view0

# 7. Compressed answer

If your question is simply **“where do I set it up?”**, the answer is:

- **Agent Builder** to design it, citeturn537312view3
- **ChatKit** to embed it in your app, citeturn259771search0turn259771search5

- **Apps SDK + MCP** to make it available inside ChatGPT, citeturn583623view3turn583623view1
- **Realtime API** for voice, citeturn608284view1
- **computer use** for UI-driven tasks. citeturn608284view2

# Practical Example — Data Engineering Project

Let us take a **realistic project** close to your background.

## Example Scenario

A company has:

- **Source system** → Sales orders
- **Target system** → Data warehouse
- **Need** → Daily ETL / data engineering pipeline
- **Problem** → Failures happen, data mismatches happen, business asks questions, logs are scattered

Now you want to understand:

> how **AI Agent → LLM → MCP → other systems** work together

---

# 1. First, the roles clearly

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| **AI Agent** | Worker that performs steps |
| **LLM** | Brain that understands language, logs, intent, patterns |
| **MCP** | Control layer that connects tools and manages context/rules |
| **Other systems** | Real systems like SQL, Airflow, Databricks, BigQuery, email, tickets, Slack, Sheets |

---

# 2. One-line architecture

```text
User / Trigger
   ↓
AI Agent
   ↓
LLM for understanding / reasoning
   ↓
MCP for tool access + context + control
   ↓
Other systems (SQL / ETL / logs / tickets / reports)
   ↓
Back to Agent
   ↓
Human-readable output / action
```

---

# 3. Real project example

## Project Goal

Every morning, check whether yesterday’s sales pipeline loaded correctly.

Pipeline:

```text
Oracle / App DB
   ↓
Extract
   ↓
Transform
   ↓
BigQuery / Snowflake / DW table
   ↓
Business report
```

Business question:

> “Did yesterday’s load complete correctly? If not, where is the issue?”

---

# 4. Traditional way vs AI-enabled way

## Traditional way

A data engineer does this manually:

1. Open scheduler tool
2. Check failed job
3. Open logs
4. Check row counts
5. Run SQL
6. Compare source vs target
7. Send email/update ticket

---

## AI-enabled way

System flow:

1. **Scheduler triggers**
2. **AI Agent starts investigation**
3. **LLM reads logs / understands failure**
4. **MCP connects to tools safely**
5. **Other systems return data**
6. **AI Agent prepares summary / creates ticket / alerts human**

---

# 5. Step-by-step detailed flow

## Step 1 — Trigger happens

This can come from:

- Airflow job failure
- Daily schedule at 7:00 AM
- Business user asks in chat:
  - “Why is yesterday’s sales missing?”

### What is happening here?

This is **not yet LLM thinking**.  
This is just a **trigger**.

Example:

```text
Trigger: sales_daily_load failed at 06:12
Date: 2026-03-26
Pipeline: SALES_FACT_LOAD
```

---

## Step 2 — AI Agent receives the goal

The **AI Agent** is the active worker.

It receives something like:

```text
Goal:
Investigate failure of SALES_FACT_LOAD for 2026-03-26.
Find likely cause, evidence, and next action.
```

### Agent role here

The agent decides workflow steps such as:

1. Get job status
2. Read logs
3. Check source count
4. Check target count
5. Check last successful run
6. Summarize findings
7. Notify team

So:

> **AI Agent = workflow executor**

---

## Step 3 — Agent uses LLM to understand the problem

Now the **LLM** comes in.

Suppose log says:

```text
ORA-01555 snapshot too old
Step failed: extract_customer_orders
Rows processed before failure: 2,145,220
```

The raw log is technical.

The LLM helps convert that into useful understanding:

### LLM does things like:

- interpret the error
- identify likely cause
- classify severity
- turn logs into human meaning
- generate SQL/checklist/query suggestions

### Example

Raw log:
```text
ORA-01555 snapshot too old
```

LLM interpretation:
```text
Likely extract query ran too long and Oracle undo data was overwritten before query completed.
Possible causes:
1. Source DB pressure
2. Query inefficiency
3. Large data volume
```

So:

> **LLM = understanding engine**

It does **reasoning and interpretation**, not direct system control by itself.

---

# 6. Where MCP enters

Now the agent needs real data from real tools.

The LLM alone cannot magically access everything.  
This is where **MCP** comes in.

## MCP role in this example

MCP provides structured access to:

- scheduler logs
- database query tools
- ticketing systems
- documentation
- runbooks
- Slack / email
- dashboard tools

And importantly, MCP can enforce rules like:

- which system can be queried
- what credentials/tool are allowed
- whether write action is allowed
- what context should be carried across steps

So:

> **MCP = controlled bridge between AI and tools**

---

# 7. Practical flow with actual steps

## Scenario Data

Let us say yesterday’s sales load failed.

### Systems available

| System | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Airflow | Scheduler/job status |
| Oracle | Source sales data |
| BigQuery | Target warehouse |
| Jira | Incident ticket |
| Slack | Notification |
| Runbook docs | Standard resolution guide |

---

## Step 7.1 — Agent asks MCP for Airflow status

The agent says:

```text
Get status and logs for SALES_FACT_LOAD for 2026-03-26
```

### MCP does:

- connects to Airflow tool
- fetches job status
- fetches logs
- returns structured output

Example result:

```text
Job: SALES_FACT_LOAD
Status: Failed
Failure step: EXTRACT_ORDERS
Time: 06:12
Error: ORA-01555 snapshot too old
```

---

## Step 7.2 — Agent sends logs to LLM

Now the agent asks LLM:

```text
Interpret this failure and suggest next checks.
```

LLM response:

```text
This is likely a source-side extraction issue.
Recommended next checks:
1. Compare source volume with recent days
2. Check extract query duration
3. Check whether source system had abnormal activity
4. Verify target table received partial load
```

---

## Step 7.3 — Agent asks MCP to query source system

The agent now wants evidence.

Through MCP, it uses the database query tool.

Example source SQL:

```sql
select count(*)
from source_orders
where order_date = date '2026-03-26';
```

Suppose result:

```text
Source count = 2,987,450
```

---

## Step 7.4 — Agent asks MCP to query target system

Now target check:

```sql
select count(*)
from dw.fact_sales
where sales_date = date '2026-03-26';
```

Suppose result:

```text
Target count = 0
```

Or maybe partial:

```text
Target count = 1,102,334
```

Now agent knows whether:

- nothing loaded
- partial load happened
- duplicate risk exists

---

## Step 7.5 — Agent asks MCP for historical comparison

This is important in data engineering.

Query last 7 days source counts:

| Date | Source Count |
|---|---:|
| 2026-03-19 | 2,101,220 |
| 2026-03-20 | 2,089,110 |
| 2026-03-21 | 2,140,921 |
| 2026-03-22 | 2,115,442 |
| 2026-03-23 | 2,132,901 |
| 2026-03-24 | 2,155,982 |
| 2026-03-25 | 2,148,760 |
| 2026-03-26 | 2,987,450 |

LLM can now infer:

> Volume spike is unusually high.  
> Error may be linked to query/runtime pressure caused by data increase.

---

# 8. Full interaction chain

Now let us show the exact flow you asked:

## **AI Agent → LLM → MCP → other system**

---

## A. AI Agent

The agent owns the mission.

Example internal task:

```text
Investigate failed sales pipeline and produce actionable summary.
```

It breaks work into sub-steps.

---

The LLM helps at points like:

- understanding logs
- deciding which checks matter
- interpreting count differences
- converting technical issues into business language

```text

Error + counts + history

Output:
Likely root cause = source extract stress due to high volume spike
Confidence = medium
Recommended action = rerun with partitioned extraction
```

---

## C. MCP

MCP enables safe tool use.

Without MCP, the LLM is just “thinking.”

With MCP, the system can actually do things like:

- fetch Airflow run info
- run source SQL
- run target SQL
- read runbook
- create Jira ticket
- post to Slack

MCP also carries context:

```text
Pipeline = SALES_FACT_LOAD
Date = 2026-03-26

Environment = PROD
```

This means the agent does not need to “re-explain everything” each step.

---

## D. Other systems

These are the actual enterprise systems:

- Airflow
- Oracle
- BigQuery
- Databricks
- Control-M
- Jira
- ServiceNow
- Slack
- Email
- SharePoint
- Runbook wiki

These systems do the real operational work.

# 9. Example end-to-end execution

## User / scheduler says:

> “Check if yesterday sales load is healthy.”

---

## Agent step sequence

### Step 1
Fetch Airflow run status

**Result:** Failed

### Step 2
Read failure logs

**Result:** ORA-01555 at extract step
